questions.corrige_markdown:
Completed table:

| No | Test procedure | Observation | Inference |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) | To 2 cm$^3$ of solution X add 5 drops of NaOH(aq) and warm | A colourless pungent gas is evolved. The gas turns damp red litmus paper blue | The gas is **ammonia**: presence of **$\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ (ammonium) ions** |
| (ii) | To 2 cm$^3$ of solution X add 2 drops of $\mathrm{BaCl_2(aq)}$ followed by dilute HCl(aq) | **A white precipitate forms and does not dissolve** in the dilute HCl | Presence of $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ ions (barium sulphate, $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_4}$) |
| (iii) | To 2 cm$^3$ of solution Y add 2 drops of NaOH(aq) | **A dirty green precipitate** forms, insoluble in excess NaOH | Presence of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ ions ($\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe(OH)_2}$) |
| (iv) | To 2 cm$^3$ of solution Y add a few drops of $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ followed by dilute $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ | A white precipitate is formed (insoluble in the dilute nitric acid) | Presence of **$\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (chloride) ions** ($\mathrm{Ag^+} + \mathrm{Cl^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl}$) |
| (v) | **Flame test:** dip a clean platinum (or nichrome) wire, moistened with concentrated HCl, into Z and hold it in the non-luminous Bunsen flame | Z gives a brick red flame colour | Presence of **$\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ (calcium) ions** |
| (vi) | A solid sample of Z strongly heated in a test tube | **Brown fumes** of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ are evolved (and a colourless gas that relights a glowing splint) | $\mathrm{NO_2}$ evolved: presence of $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ (nitrate) ions |

For (i) the equation is $\mathrm{NH_4^+} + \mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_3} + \mathrm{H_2O}$ (warming drives off the ammonia gas).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Give the chemical identity of

X

Y

Z *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **X** contains $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ and $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$: it is **ammonium sulphate, $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$**.
- **Y** contains $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$: it is **iron(II) chloride, $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$**.
- **Z** contains $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$: it is **calcium nitrate, $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$** (on heating: $2\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CaO} + 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$).

questions.corrige_markdown:
| Mixture | Technique of separation |
|---|---|
| Kerosine and water | **Separating funnel** (the two liquids do not mix; kerosine, the less dense liquid, forms the upper layer and the water is run off from below) |
| **Salt solution (salt and water), or ethanol and water** | Simple distillation |
| **A mixture of coloured dyes (for example the dyes in a black ink or in a plant extract)** | Paper chromatography |
| Groundnut and its peelings | **Winnowing** (the light peelings are blown away; sieving or hand picking is also accepted) |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) In order to dilute an acid, a student added 410 cm$^3$ of distilled water to 10 cm$^3$ of concentrated sulphuric acid. State and justify what is wrong with this procedure.

(ii) Why is it advisable to wear eye goggles when working in the laboratory? *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Water was added to the acid.** The correct procedure is to add the **concentrated acid slowly to the water, stirring all the time**. Diluting concentrated sulphuric acid releases a large amount of heat; if water is poured onto the acid it can boil suddenly, because the water is less dense and floats on the acid, and the mixture spits out hot drops of corrosive acid that can burn the skin and eyes. When the acid is poured into a large volume of water, the water absorbs the heat safely.

(ii) Eye goggles **protect the eyes from splashes of corrosive or harmful chemicals, from flying particles and from broken glass**, since damage to the eyes may be permanent.
